source.title: Non-linear Interventions on Large Language Models

record.tranche_reason: The paper argues for non-linear feature representations and tests refusal-bypass interventions, but it does not test or rely on superposition, feature competition for representational capacity, SAE features, or the geometry of superposed features.
record.gate_note: The reported refusal-bypass outcomes are produced by deliberately intervening on the model. They do not measure naturally occurring superposition or any of the six claim versions. The adjacent intervention-method comparisons are recorded as findings under versions ["none"].
record.test_reason: The paper proposes and evaluates a learned non-linear intervention for refusal bypass on Llama3-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. It argues against strict reliance on the Linear Representation Hypothesis but never measures superposition, feature counts against dimensions, polysemanticity, SAE features, or the dimensionality of superposed features. Its results are steering scores from interventions the authors induce on purpose. The closest version is V6, via the claim that the refusal feature is non-linear. That feature is still a single coordinate (k=1) of an invertible map and is not shown to be superposed or multi-dimensional, so V6 is not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct, with one refinement. The authors claim StrongREJECT scores comparable to the linear baselines (DIM, RDO), not higher, while editing one site with an L2 norm over two orders of magnitude smaller. They infer a genuinely non-linear refusal feature residing mainly in the middle layers.
record.recipe_differences: The study learns an invertible non-linear feature map for refusal-bypass steering and compares it with linear refusal-steering baselines; it does not reproduce a superposition experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: Intervention layer: the method is largely ineffective at early layers, peaks at middle layers, and declines at later layers.

fits_no_version.finding: Under the same objective and pipeline, a non-linear (i-ResNet) feature map gives much higher StrongREJECT than a linear-constrained map: 0.813 vs 0.010 on Llama, 0.760 vs 0.072 on Qwen. It also beats linear edits at all loss sites: 0.813 vs 0.689 and 0.760 vs 0.415. The authors take this as evidence that refusal is governed by a non-linear feature located mainly in the middle layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some behaviour-governing features in LLMs (e.g., refusal) are encoded non-linearly, so linear directional interventions capture them less precisely than learned non-linear maps.

record.problems: The experiments cover two models. No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported. The paper states that the RDO ActAdd result on Qwen was judged unreliable and excluded from the figure and table.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-version results were left out. The paper also reports intervention magnitudes and a layer sweep, but these are outcomes of deliberately induced refusal-bypass steering and do not measure the claim versions.

untested.parts: All: no toy models, no sparsity sweep, no geometry of feature directions.
All: no capacity or feature-importance analysis, no neuron polysemanticity.
All: polysemantic neurons are not studied.
All: no distributed-neuron analysis and no SAE or dictionary learning.
All: no SAE features are examined.
Whether superposed features are 1-D directions or multi-dimensional. The study learns a single (k=1) non-linear coordinate for refusal and does not examine superposition or feature dimensionality.

record.verdict_notes: Preprint, two models, no uncertainty reported. The RDO ActAdd result on Qwen (0.020) was excluded as unreliable. The paper does not cite Toy Models of Superposition, and its link to the phenomenon runs only through the Linear Representation Hypothesis debate (Engels et al. 2025). The 'discusses' relation is generous, since the paper never discusses superposition explicitly.

versions.untested_parts: Whether sparse features outnumber dimensions, overlap as nearly orthogonal directions, or show sparsity-dependent transitions and regular geometry.
Whether limited capacity causes polysemanticity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise without capacity pressure or what they imply about superposition.
Whether LLM features are distributed across neurons or recoverable with sparse autoencoders.
Whether SAE features are complete, stable, canonical units of model representations.
Whether superposed features are one-dimensional directions or multidimensional features.
